## Overview and grading

### What you'll practice

In this graded assignment,
you'll run a multi-step RNA-seq workflow on the @garrigós2025 data,
from raw reads to transcript counts.
You'll organize it like we discussed in week 10:
with single-step shell scripts that you submit as Slurm batch jobs,
and a Markdown "protocol" with the code to run these scripts in order.
Along the way, you'll quantify gene expression with Salmon,
and you'll summarize the results of all steps in a single MultiQC report.

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Nov 8^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: Like for GA3 and GA4,
  you will submit your assignment by tagging the instructors in an Issue
  in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.

::: callout-note
#### Oral examination
As explained in [GA3](GA3.qmd#oral-exam),
each of you will have **one** short oral examination, for one of GA3, GA4, or GA5.
If you haven't had yours yet, it will be for this assignment,
in which case you should also be able to explain any code that genAI wrote for you.
:::

## Instructions

### General

- **Two Markdown files**:
  - Like before, we provide a **template** `README.md` with a section for each question,
    where you add your answers (see "Setting up" below).
    Add commands and their output only where the template asks for them.
  - Separately, you'll build the **protocol** for your workflow in a file `protocol.md`,
    which should contain the final code to run all steps in order,
    like the [protocol example in w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#a-protocol-example).
    You don't need to repeat this code in your `README.md`.

- For **each step** where you run a shell script one or more times, you should:
  1. Submit the shell script as one or more batch jobs
  2. Monitor the progress of the job(s)
  3. When they are done, check the Slurm log files and the output files
  4. If you detect failures, try to figure out what went wrong, and rerun
  5. Move the Slurm log files of the successful run(s) into a `logs` dir within
     the script's output dir (the scripts create these `logs` dirs for you;
     this is a small addition that you haven't seen in scripts so far).

- **Commit** your files to your Git repo as you go along,
  using informative commit messages: commit at least once per Part (A--F).

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
The workflow is similar to
[the protocol example in w10b](../week10/w10b_slurm2.qmd#a-protocol-example),
but not identical!
To get some genuine practice, and to avoid copying the wrong things,
we recommend not to copy-paste code from that lecture page.
:::

### Part B: Read trimming

06. Take a look at the `trimgalore.sh` script,
    which is similar to the one you worked on in GA4.
    Add a loop to your protocol that runs the script once per sample, run it,
    and monitor your jobs.
    Did all batch jobs succeed, and how did you check that?

    ::: callout-tip
    #### What to do when jobs fail
    - Try to figure out what went wrong (you can ask Claude for help if you want),
      and rerun the failed jobs.
    - Remove Slurm log files of failed runs once you've figured out the problem.
    - Your protocol should only contain the code for the successful run(s).
    - Your README should report any problems you encountered and how you solved them.
    :::

    ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
    #### The TrimGalore output files _(Click to expand)_
    Unlike the TrimGalore script from GA4,
    this script renames the trimmed FASTQ files to the same names as the input files,
    like `S63_R1.fastq.gz`.

    (But since TrimGalore runs FastQC on the trimmed files before this renaming,
    the FastQC output files still have names like `S63_R1_val_1_fastqc.html`.)
    :::

### Part C: Transcript quantification with Salmon

In week 11, the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline first aligned the reads
to the reference **genome** with STAR,
and then used Salmon to quantify gene expression based on those alignments.
Here, you'll use Salmon on its own:
it can also directly map the reads to the reference **transcriptome**,
i.e. to the sequences of all annotated transcripts,
and estimate how many reads came from each transcript.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More about Salmon's mapping approach _(Click to expand)_
This approach is often loosely called **pseudo-alignment**
(Salmon's current method is technically called "selective alignment"),
because it doesn't produce full read alignments.
Compared to aligning to the genome, it has the following advantages and disadvantages:

- Pseudo-alignment is **much faster** and needs much less memory.
- It doesn't need to be "splice-aware" like STAR:
  since transcript sequences don't contain introns,
  reads from mature mRNAs match them without gaps.
- But you **can only quantify known transcripts**,
  i.e. those in the annotation, and you don't get alignment (BAM) files,
  which you would need for other purposes,
  like visualizing alignments or calling variants.
:::

Like with most aligners, Salmon needs an **index** of the reference sequences.
You'll first create this index, and then use it in the quantification step.

07. **Create the index**. Take a look at the `salmon_index.sh` script,
    add the code to run it to your protocol, and run it.
    (Only a single index is needed, so you'll run this script just once.)
    When it's done, report how long it took to create the index,
    and how large the index dir is.

08. **Quantify the reads**. Now, add code to your protocol to run the `salmon_quant.sh` script,
    for one sample at a time, to quantify the trimmed reads using the index
    (note: the third argument is the dir of the index, not a file).
    Then, run it.

09. Take a look at Salmon's main output file, `quant.sf`, for sample `S63`, and use the
    [Salmon documentation on its output files](https://salmon.readthedocs.io/en/latest/file_formats.html){target="_blank"}
    to understand what the columns in this file mean, especially `NumReads`.
    Then, write a command that prints the 3 rows of its `quant.sf` file
    with the **highest `NumReads` values**
    (see the [self-study section on sorting by column](../bonus/shell-data-tools.qmd#sorting-by-column-numerically)).

10. For the most abundant transcript you found in the previous question,
    **find its FASTA header** in the reference transcriptome file,
    and report which gene it belongs to.

    ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
    #### Transcript versus gene counts _(Click to expand)_
    Salmon has quantified the number of reads that came from each transcript.
    But for most analyses, such as a differential expression analysis,
    you'll want counts per gene, not per transcript.
    Using a mapping from transcripts to genes, which you can e.g. extract from a GTF file,
    you can sum the transcript counts for each gene to get gene-level counts.
    :::

11. Salmon reports the **mapping rate**,
    i.e. the percentage of reads that it could assign to a transcript,
    in the file `logs/salmon_quant.log` within each sample's output dir.
    Write a command that prints the mapping rate for all samples at once.
    Which sample has the lowest mapping rate?

    <details><summary> {{< fa info-circle >}} _Click here for a hint_</summary>
    You'll need a glob pattern to match the `salmon_quant.log` files in all sample dirs,
    and can use `grep` to extract the mapping rate from each log file.

    As for the globbing:
    so far, you've used the `*` wildcard to match file names within a single dir.
    But a `*` can also stand in for a dir name anywhere in a path.
    For example, the following lists the contents of the `logs` dirs
    of all your workflow steps so far:

    ```bash
    ls results/*/logs
    ```

    (For more on this, see the
    [self-study section on globbing across dirs](../bonus/shell.qmd#globbing-across-dirs).)

    As for `grep`: when you give `grep` multiple files,
    it starts each output line with the name of the file that the line came from ---
    which here tells you the sample ID.
    </details>

### Part D: Summarizing all steps with MultiQC

In GA3, you ran MultiQC on FastQC output only.
But MultiQC recognizes the output of hundreds of bioinformatics programs,
including TrimGalore and Salmon,
and it can summarize all of these in a single report ---
like the report that you saw for the nf-core _rnaseq_ pipeline in week 11.
So here, you'll run MultiQC once, at the end of the workflow,
on your entire `results` dir.

12. The `multiqc.sh` script is much like what you wrote in GA3,
    and was written to be run directly with `bash`.
    **Update it** so that it is also suitable to be submitted as a batch job:
    add `#SBATCH` lines with the OSC project,
    a descriptive Slurm log file name, and email notification for failed jobs.
    Then, commit the updated script.

13. Add code to your protocol to **run MultiQC** with `results` as the input dir,
    and `results/multiqc` as the output dir, and run it.
    In the Slurm log, MultiQC reports the number of reports it found for each program.
    For each program, explain why it found this number of reports.

14. Download the MultiQC report, and open it in your browser.
    Take a few minutes to explore the report.
    In the **General Statistics** table at the top,
    which sample has the lowest Salmon mapping rate,
    and does this match your answer to question 11?

15. In the "Trim Galore" section of the report,
    look at the "**Adapter Length Distribution**" plot.
    What, approximately, are the most common adapter lengths trimmed from the reads?
    Does this surprise you?
    Either way, why do you think these lengths are the most common?

16. **Ask Claude** about one aspect of the MultiQC report that you don't (entirely)
    understand; ask follow-up questions if needed.
    In the README, summarize what you asked and learned from Claude's answer,
    in your own words.
    _Optional_: ask additional questions, if you have more points of confusion.

    (You can point to the file with the `@`-notation,
    or simply open it in the editor in default (raw) mode so it's automatically
    added as context. Even if you do neither, Claude will likely figure out
    which file you're referring to.)

### Part E: Improving the workflow with genAI

17. Your protocol should allow someone else (or a future you!) to rerun your
    entire workflow.
    **Ask Claude to review** your `protocol.md` and the scripts in `scripts/`,
    and ask it to point out what is missing, unclear, or inconsistent,
    and how you could improve reproducibility.
    (If it gives an overwhelming number of suggestions,
    you can for example ask it to focus on the most important ones in a follow-up
    question or a separate conversation.)

    Discuss at least three of Claude's suggestions in your README,
    explaining whether you agree or disagree with each one, and why.

18. For at least one suggestion you agree with,
    address it in your protocol and/or scripts, and commit.
    Describe what you changed in your README.
